title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.
summary: This work presents a comprehensive optimal-control framework to design high-fidelity controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. By systematically modeling intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence (including fast and slow dephasing), the authors achieved fast gates with extremely low error rates. The results establish a robust design methodology that minimizes the need for constant recalibration as quantum processors scale.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical challenge of developing quantum gates for superconducting qubits that are simultaneously high-fidelity, fast, and robust against environmental noise, which is crucial for scaling quantum processors.
main_result: They achieved 12-ns controlled-Z gates with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2	imes10^{-5}$ level, demonstrating that gate performance can be maintained below $10^{-3}$ even with significant noise sources.
method: The authors developed a unified optimal-control framework that systematically incorporates both intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms (energy relaxation and dephasing) into the gate design.
model_or_system: The system uses directly coupled, frequency-tunable superconducting transmon qubits. The analysis involves modeling the system Hamiltonian and projecting the evolution onto the computational subspace while incorporating noise models calibrated against experimental measurements.
key_observables: Gate infidelity, intrinsic error suppression level, and noise tolerance margins.
important_parameters: Gate speed (12-ns), intrinsic error level ($2	imes10^{-5}$), transmon asymmetry parameter ($a_{EJ}$), and decoherence rates ($T_1, T_{\phi}$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the direct-coupling architecture, and certain derivations rely on approximations regarding the smallness of leakage probabilities and the low-order nature of error contributions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the decoupling of even-quanta and odd-quanta states, detailing leakage pathways from computational basis states to non-computational states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the need for robust gates, to developing the optimal-control framework that decomposes errors, to constructing realistic noise models, and finally presenting results showing how asymmetry and sweet-spot engineering balance speed, fidelity, and noise resilience.
why_interesting: It provides a highly practical, physics-informed methodology for designing quantum gates by explicitly balancing coherent control errors against dissipative noise channels, which is a key concern in open quantum systems.
